# C++ hash tables and R methods

`RSSet` and `RSDictionary` are public classes for storing RObjC objects.
They use C++ hash tables to find elements and keys, while each object's `hash()` and `isEqual()` determine the meaning of hashes and equality.
This note (07) follows the path from the R classes to C++ storage and the callbacks from C++ to R methods.
For the public API, see the [collections guide](guide_07_Collections.Rmd); for the method contracts, see the [equality and hashing guide](guide_08_Hash_isEqual.Rmd).

## Three implementation layers

The public classes `RSSet`, `RSMutableSet`, `RSDictionary`, and `RSMutableDictionary` handle input validation, mutable and immutable operations, copying, and coding.
The internal `RSConcreteSet` and `RSConcreteDictionary` classes call Rcpp functions and hold external pointers to C++ objects.
`NativeSet` and `NativeDictionary` perform the actual insertion, lookup, and removal.

```text
Public class method
    → RSConcreteSet / RSConcreteDictionary
    → Rcpp set_* / dictionary_* function
    → C++ unordered_set / unordered_map
    → RSObjectHash / RSObjectEqual
    → RObjC object's hash() / isEqual()
```

`NativeSet` uses `std::unordered_set<SEXP, RSObjectHash, RSObjectEqual>`.
`NativeDictionary` uses `std::unordered_map<SEXP, SEXP, RSObjectHash, RSObjectEqual>`, with only the key participating in hash lookup.
The value is stored in the same entry, but its `hash()` does not determine the entry's location.

## `hash()` and `isEqual()` callbacks

In `src/RSObjectHash.cpp`, `RSObjectHash` treats the received `SEXP` as an R environment and calls its `hash` method.
`RSObjectEqual` calls `isEqual` on one of two `SEXP` values, passing the other as an argument.
Rcpp converts the results to C++ `std::size_t` and `bool`, respectively.

```cpp
std::size_t RSObjectHash::operator()(SEXP key) const {
  Rcpp::Environment env(key);
  Rcpp::Function fn = env["hash"];
  return Rcpp::as<std::size_t>(fn());
}

bool RSObjectEqual::operator()(SEXP a, SEXP b) const {
  Rcpp::Environment env(a);
  Rcpp::Function fn = env["isEqual"];
  return Rcpp::as<bool>(fn(b));
}
```

On the R side, the public classes validate a `hash()` result as a single, nonmissing integer before insertion.
End a custom `hash()` implementation with `robjc_normalize_hash()` to avoid the `NA_integer_` bit pattern.
Equal objects must produce equal hash values.
The table uses `isEqual()` to distinguish candidates whose hash values collide.

```{r}
library(robjc)

stored <- RSString$new("id")
lookup <- RSString$new("id")
stopifnot(!identical(stored, lookup))
stopifnot(stored$isEqual(lookup))
stopifnot(identical(stored$hash(), lookup$hash()))

set <- RSSet$new(list(stored))
stopifnot(identical(set$member(lookup), stored))

value <- RSNumber$new(7L)
dictionary <- RSMutableDictionary$new()
dictionary$setObjectForKey(value, stored)
stopifnot(identical(dictionary$objectForKey(lookup), value))
```

`lookup` is a different instance from the stored `stored`, yet the hash and equality contract lets the tables find the same element or key.
A hash table typically examines fewer candidates than a linear search, but collisions and the cost of callbacks to R methods require separate performance assessment.
Avoid implementations that depend on the number or order of C++ calls to `hash()` or `isEqual()`.

## Copying and retaining at insertion

Set retains a reference to an inserted object without copying it.
For an RObjC instance used as a Dictionary key, the public class calls `key$copy()` before passing it to C++.
For class or protocol generators used as keys, it keeps the same generator reference.
Dictionary values are stored by reference without copying.
These rules belong to the public classes, not to `RSConcreteSet` or the C++ hash table.

To keep stored R objects alive as C++ `SEXP` values, `NativeSet` and `NativeDictionary` register elements or key-value pairs in an R precious multi-set.
They release obsolete references on removal or replacement and release the multi-set when native storage is destroyed.
This prevents R's garbage collector from reclaiming an object that remains only in a C++ table.

## Keep hash-relevant state stable

Set elements and Dictionary keys must retain stable state relevant to hashing and equality after insertion.
If a changed `hash()` result directs lookup to another location, an existing entry may no longer be found.
Changing only the outcome of `isEqual()` can also invalidate duplicate checks and lookup results.
Dictionary calls `copy()` to separate key state, but users still need to preserve stability if a custom `copy()` returns `self` or the copied object remains mutable.

```{r}
stopifnot(identical(dictionary$objectForKey(RSString$new("id")), value))
```

The hash tables are not ordered collections.
Do not assume an order for Set elements or Dictionary keys; use an Array alongside them when insertion order matters.
Keyed Archive does not save an external pointer directly.
Instead, the public class's `encodeWithCoder()` writes logical elements or key-value pairs, as described in [note 08](tech_08_Archiving.Rmd).
